title: Gather the scattered
hook: sound the great shofar for freedom and gather the scattered

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing of the years. Your line was a year that feeds you. Did one piece of work get done with care? Today, the Amidah turns from the private to the whole people. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

Pull up a map of where Jewish families have lived. Babylon and Baghdad. Cordoba and Toledo. Fez, Cairo, Aleppo, Sana'a. Vilna, Kraków, Odessa. Cochin on the coast of India. Then Brooklyn, Buenos Aires, Johannesburg, Melbourne. One Shabbat table can hold a recipe from Aleppo and a lullaby from Vilna. Some families carry two or three of those names in their own story. In all of those places, every weekday, the same line of the Amidah has spoken directly to that map.
screen: `BABYLON, CORDOBA, FEZ, VILNA.` → `COCHIN, BROOKLYN, BUENOS AIRES.` → `A LINE THAT SPEAKS TO THE MAP.`

segments.voice: The tenth blessing says: sound the great shofar for our freedom. Raise a banner to gather our exiles, and gather us together from the four corners of the earth. Blessed are You, who gathers the dispersed of Your people Israel. The great shofar comes from the prophet Isaiah. In the old Jewish translation: "it shall come to pass in that day, that a great horn shall be blown," and the lost and the scattered come home to worship in Jerusalem. The banner comes from Isaiah too: a signal raised high, so people far away can see where to come. Notice the first word of the blessing is not gather. It's teka: blow. The shofar is the sound of the Jubilee year, when slaves went free and land returned to its families. So freedom comes first, then gathering. Here the requests turn toward the whole people's future, from my troubles to our story. The Talmud, in Megillah 17b, says it follows the blessing of the years because a prophet promised that when the land bears fruit again, the exiles will be near. Jews have said these words in Baghdad and Vilna and Cochin, far from Jerusalem. In modern times, some see the return of Jews to the land of Israel in this light, and others read the blessing as pointing to a future not yet here. Either way, every weekday, scattered people ask to be gathered.
screen: `TEKA: BLOW THE GREAT SHOFAR.` · `RAISE A BANNER FOR THE EXILES.` · `FREEDOM FIRST, THEN GATHERING.` · `FROM MY TROUBLES TO OUR STORY.` · then, large: `GATHER THE SCATTERED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think of someone far away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love who lives far from you: a sibling across the country, a grandparent in another land, a friend who moved and slowly went quiet. Picture where they are right now, what time it is there, what they might be doing. Imagine, for a moment, the whole table together again. If you pray, you can hold them in this blessing. The bell holds the time.
Teka. Blow: the Amidah's tenth blessing opens with the shofar's blast, then asks to gather the exiles from the four corners of the earth.
Your line: freedom comes first, then gathering. Today, reach out to the far-away person you pictured, and make one plan, however small, to be in the same place. Day five hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Teka beshofar, the request to gather the exiles, is the tenth blessing of the weekday Amidah, said three times a day; communities differ in how they relate it to the modern State of Israel.

original.note: Hebrew: sound the great shofar. the opening words of the tenth blessing.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old line about going back to Israel.
what it means: freedom first, then gathering: scattered people asking, every weekday, to be one people again.
what a scholar hears: Isaiah 27:13 for the great horn, Isaiah 11:12 for the banner and four corners; the Jubilee shofar of Leviticus 25; Megillah 17b on Ezekiel 36:8.
